quoted_clause: the meaningful per-step data movement is a TP all-reduce of the per-layer activations (tens of MBs, not GBs) plus the KV cache fragment exchange in disaggregated serving
observed: The sentence structure 'per-step data movement is [A] plus [B]' implies both A (TP all-reduce) and B (KV cache exchange) occur every decode step. KV cache transfer in P/D disaggregation occurs once per sequence at the prefill-to-decode boundary, not per step. The later clause 'when a P-D sequence transfers' corrects the timing but arrives after the misleading framing has already been established.
evidence: P/D disaggregation transfers KV once per sequence when moving from prefill to decode pool. TP all-reduce occurs per layer per decode step. These are fundamentally different frequencies. The grammatical structure places both under a single 'per-step' qualifier.
root_cause: Sentence structure conflates two operations of different frequency under one 'per-step' qualifier.
correction: Restructure to separate frequencies: 'Per decode step, the meaningful data movement is a TP all-reduce of per-layer activations (tens of MBs). In disaggregated serving, there is also a one-time KV transfer when a sequence moves from prefill to decode — e.g., ~35 GB of KV moved over NVLink ...'
acceptance_test: After correction, a reader cannot reasonably interpret the KV transfer as occurring every decode step.

quoted_clause: it delivers the lowest per-iteration communication time, which translates to higher throughput per dollar over the life of the cluster
observed: Unqualified causal claim: lower communication time is said to 'translate to' higher throughput per dollar. This requires that (a) communication is a significant fraction of iteration time, (b) the NVSwitch cost premium is offset by time savings, and (c) the workload is communication-intensive. None of these conditions is stated.
evidence: If communication is 5% of iteration time, a 2× communication speedup yields only ~5% iteration improvement, unlikely to offset NVSwitch's cost premium over RoCE. The claim holds only under specific workload and cost conditions that are not mentioned.
root_cause: Causal chain from communication time to economic outcome stated without intermediate conditions.
correction: Qualify: '...which can translate to higher throughput per dollar when communication is a significant fraction of iteration time and the cost premium is justified by the workload's communication intensity.'
acceptance_test: The claim includes at least one condition under which the causal chain holds.

page_hint: Ch9 §7 What We Still Don't Know — Cross-domain generalization
quoted_clause: Diagonal dominant tensors, sparse gradients, or structured compression may exhibit different effective bandwidths because the traffic pattern across links is less uniform
observed: For dense collectives (ring all-reduce), tensor shape and content do not affect the traffic pattern across links — the ring algorithm sends fixed-size chunks regardless of tensor content. Only the total byte count matters. The claim that 'diagonal dominant tensors' produce a 'less uniform' traffic pattern is incorrect for dense representations. The claim is valid only for sparse/compressed representations where the byte count and potentially the access pattern change.
evidence: In a ring all-reduce, each rank sends (N-1)/N × M bytes in fixed-size chunks. The chunk size and count depend on M (total bytes), not on the tensor's internal structure. A diagonal-dominant dense tensor of the same shape as a uniform tensor produces identical link traffic.
root_cause: Conflation of tensor content/structure with representation format. Dense tensor shape does not affect collective traffic pattern; only sparse/compressed representations change byte count.
correction: Scope the claim to sparse and compressed representations: 'Sparse or compressed representations of gradient tensors may exhibit different effective bandwidths because the reduced byte count and potentially non-uniform access patterns change link utilization. For dense collectives, only the total byte count matters, not the tensor's internal structure.'
acceptance_test: The claim does not imply that dense tensor shape affects collective traffic pattern.

quoted_clause: Measured effective bandwidth is typically 40–60% of peak
observed: General empirical claim presented without source or evidence label. The book uses evidence labels elsewhere ([ILLUSTRATIVE], [DERIVED], etc.).
evidence: No citation, measurement reference, or evidence label accompanies this claim. It reads as a factual assertion.
root_cause: Unlabeled empirical generalization in Common Mistakes section.
correction: Add an evidence label: 'Measured effective bandwidth is typically 40–60% of peak [ILLUSTRATIVE]' or provide a source for the range.
acceptance_test: The claim carries an evidence label or a citation.

evidence: No citation, measurement reference, or evidence label accompanies this claim.

quoted_clause: the ideal whole-context limit of 17 slots per host gives ⌈10,000/17⌉=589 hosts
observed: The number 17 is used as a given without derivation or cross-reference to where it was established. The reader cannot verify this number from the current chapter.
evidence: No section reference, equation reference, or derivation accompanies '17 slots per host.' The arithmetic 10000/17 = 588.24, ceiling = 589 is correct, but the input 17 is unverifiable from this chapter.
root_cause: Missing cross-reference to the chapter/section where 17 slots per host was derived.

page_hint: Ch9 §7 What We Still Don't Know — Optical interconnects
quoted_clause: pushing node‑level bandwidth higher (toward 1.8 TB/s aggregate)
observed: NVLink 5 provides 1.8 TB/s per GPU, not per node. Calling this 'node-level bandwidth' and 'aggregate' is imprecise — for an 8-GPU node, the aggregate NVLink bandwidth would be much higher (limited by switch capacity), while 1.8 TB/s is the per-GPU figure.
evidence: NVLink 5 specification: 1.8 TB/s bidirectional per GPU. For 8 GPUs, the NVSwitch fabric aggregate would be up to 8 × 1.8 = 14.4 TB/s (subject to switch limits). 'Node-level' and 'aggregate' suggest a per-node figure, but 1.8 TB/s is per-GPU.
root_cause: Per-GPU bandwidth figure described as 'node-level' and 'aggregate.'
correction: Clarify: 'pushing per-GPU NVLink bandwidth higher (toward 1.8 TB/s per GPU)' or 'pushing intra-node bandwidth higher (NVLink 5 provides 1.8 TB/s per GPU).'
acceptance_test: The bandwidth figure is correctly attributed to per-GPU or per-node scope.

page_hint: Ch9 §2 Mental Model — end of section
quoted_clause: <!-- Figure spec: mechanism-first — illustrate how all-reduce data flows through the interconnect hierarchy (PCIe → NVLink → NVSwitch → InfiniBand → Ethernet), with bandwidth numbers from the text annotated on each link. Used to explain the arithmetic in §9. Concept. -->
observed: HTML comment describes a figure showing all-reduce data flow through the interconnect hierarchy with bandwidth annotations. No corresponding figure exists in the chapter — Fig 9.1 (ring time curves), Fig 9.2 (four-rank ring SUM), and Fig 9.3 (payload layers) do not match this description.
evidence: The three figures in the chapter are: Fig 9.1 (ring all-reduce time), Fig 9.2 (collective semantics), Fig 9.3 (communication layers). None shows 'all-reduce data flows through the interconnect hierarchy (PCIe → NVLink → NVSwitch → InfiniBand → Ethernet) with bandwidth numbers.'
root_cause: Leftover figure specification for a figure that was never created, or a figure that was planned but not included.
correction: Either create the described figure (it would be pedagogically valuable — showing data flow through the physical hierarchy with bandwidth annotations) or remove the comment.
acceptance_test: Either the figure exists and matches the description, or the comment is removed.

quoted_clause: bandwidth drops ~2–3 orders of magnitude from HBM to the cluster fabric
observed: HBM3 (H100) = 3,350 GB/s. Cluster fabric (HDR) = 25 GB/s. Ratio = 3,350/25 = 134 ≈ 10^2.1. This is about 2 orders of magnitude, not 2–3. Even the slowest fabric in the table (25 GB/s) gives ~2 orders. To reach 3 orders, the fabric would need to be ~3.35 GB/s, which is not in the table.
evidence: 3350/25 = 134 ≈ 10^2.1. 3350/50 = 67 ≈ 10^1.8. The range from HBM to the slowest listed fabric is ~1.8–2.1 orders of magnitude.
root_cause: Upper bound of the order-of-magnitude range overstates the actual ratio.
correction: Change to '~2 orders of magnitude' or '~2–2.5 orders of magnitude.'
acceptance_test: The stated order-of-magnitude range matches the ratio of the table's fastest and slowest entries.

quoted_clause: when a P-D sequence transfers a ~13K-token context
observed: The mini-case uses 'P-D' (hyphen) while Chapter 10's opening uses 'P/D' (slash) for the same concept (prefill/decode disaggregation).
evidence: Ch9 §8: 'P-D sequence.' Ch10 opening: 'P/D disaggregation.' Inconsistent separator for the same term.
root_cause: Terminology inconsistency between hyphen and slash separators for prefill/decode.
correction: Unify to one form (likely 'P/D' to match the Chapter 10 usage and common convention) throughout.
acceptance_test: The prefill/decode disaggregation term uses a consistent separator across all occurrences.

page_hint: Ch9 §7 What We Still Don't Know — Adaptive collective algorithms
quoted_clause: New collectives (e.g., gradient compression, sparse all-reduce, error‑bounded approximations) claim to reduce the data volume
observed: Gradient compression, sparse all-reduce, and error-bounded approximations are not 'collectives' per se — they are compression/approximation techniques applied before or during existing collective operations (all-reduce, etc.). A 'collective' is the communication operation itself.
evidence: Gradient compression reduces the data before the all-reduce collective. Sparse all-reduce is a variant of all-reduce with sparse data. Error-bounded approximations modify the reduction. These are techniques, not new collective operations.
root_cause: Terminology imprecision — techniques applied to collectives described as 'new collectives.'
correction: Change to 'New compression and approximation techniques (e.g., gradient compression, sparse all-reduce, error-bounded approximations) claim to reduce the data volume sent by existing collectives.'
acceptance_test: The term 'collective' is reserved for communication operations (all-reduce, all-gather, etc.), not compression techniques.

quoted_clause: If the budget can accommodate NVLink‑connected hosts, keeping the all-reduce on-node
observed: 'NVLink-connected hosts' is ambiguous — NVLink connects GPUs within a host, not hosts to each other. The phrase could be misread as hosts connected by NVLink (inter-host), which doesn't exist in standard configurations.
evidence: NVLink is an intra-host GPU-to-GPU interconnect. NVSwitch is the intra-host switch fabric. Neither connects hosts to each other.
correction: Change to 'hosts with NVLink-connected GPUs' or 'NVSwitch-connected hosts' or 'hosts where GPUs are connected by NVLink.'
acceptance_test: The phrase unambiguously refers to intra-host GPU interconnect, not inter-host connection.

page_hint: Ch9 §7 What We Still Don't Know — Adaptive collective algorithms
quoted_clause: the latency per byte may increase because of compression/decompression steps
observed: 'Latency per byte' is a non-standard phrase here. Compression reduces bytes sent (decreasing transmission time) but adds computation time (increasing total time). The trade-off is about total time, not 'latency per byte.' The per-byte transmission time (1/bandwidth) doesn't change with compression.
evidence: Transmission time = bytes / bandwidth. Compression reduces bytes, so transmission time decreases. Compression computation adds time. Total time = compression time + (compressed bytes / bandwidth) + decompression time. 'Latency per byte' doesn't capture this trade-off.
root_cause: Non-standard use of 'latency per byte' to describe a computation-overhead trade-off.
correction: Change to 'the total time may increase because compression/decompression computation can offset the bandwidth savings' or 'the per-byte processing overhead may increase.'
acceptance_test: The phrase correctly describes the computation-vs-bandwidth trade-off.

page_hint: Ch9 §7 What We Still Don't Know — Cross-domain generalization
quoted_clause: Most published bandwidth measurements use square matrices (all-reduce of a gradient tensor)
observed: 'Square matrices' is not the standard description of all-reduce benchmark inputs. nccl-tests and similar benchmarks typically use 1D buffers of varying sizes, not 2D square matrices. The parenthetical '(all-reduce of a gradient tensor)' clarifies intent but the 'square matrices' phrasing is imprecise.
evidence: nccl-tests inputs are 1D arrays. The term 'square matrices' suggests 2D inputs, which is not standard for collective bandwidth benchmarks.
root_cause: Imprecise description of benchmark input format.
correction: Change to 'Most published bandwidth measurements use standard dense buffers (all-reduce of a gradient tensor)' or simply 'Most published bandwidth measurements use dense gradient tensors of standard shape.'
acceptance_test: The description of benchmark inputs matches standard collective benchmark practice.

quoted_clause: in multi-GPU topologies the traffic is split across multiple GPUs and multiple links (a two-rank collective over one path can saturate it, and the ring model of §3 carries (N−1)/N of the tensor per link)
observed: The parenthetical crams three distinct points into one sentence: (1) traffic is split across links, (2) a two-rank collective over one path CAN saturate it (seemingly contradicting point 1), (3) the ring model carries (N-1)/N per link. The resolution — that a two-rank collective has only one path, so there's no splitting — is not stated.
evidence: Point 1 says traffic is split (so you don't saturate one link). Point 2 says a two-rank case CAN saturate one path. These seem contradictory without the implicit resolution that two ranks have only one path between them.
root_cause: Three distinct logical points compressed into one parenthetical without explicit resolution of the apparent contradiction.
correction: Separate the points: 'In multi-GPU topologies, traffic is split across multiple links, so a single all-reduce typically does not saturate one link. (A two-rank collective is the exception — it has only one path and can saturate it.) The ring model of §3 carries (N-1)/N of the tensor per link.'
acceptance_test: The apparent contradiction between 'traffic is split' and 'two-rank can saturate' is explicitly resolved.

quoted_clause: A cluster of 8×H100 servers connected by NVSwitch is the highest upfront capital expenditure
observed: '8×H100 servers connected by NVSwitch' is ambiguous. NVSwitch connects GPUs within a server, not servers to each other. The phrase could be read as '8 servers connected by NVSwitch' (incorrect) or 'servers with 8 H100s each, with NVSwitch connecting GPUs within each server' (correct).
evidence: NVSwitch is an intra-server switch fabric. It does not connect servers. The intended meaning is servers with 8 H100s each, with NVSwitch providing intra-server GPU connectivity.
correction: Clarify: 'A cluster of servers, each with 8 NVSwitch-connected H100s, is the highest upfront capital expenditure' or 'A cluster of 8-GPU H100 servers with NVSwitch intra-node interconnect...'
acceptance_test: The phrase unambiguously describes intra-server GPU connectivity, not inter-server connection.
